item.title: U.S. Pensions Are Riding the A.I. Wave. For Better or Worse.
item.description:
When a researcher resigned from Anthropic out of fear that artificial intelligence might destroy all of humanity, the startling revelation panicked everyday Americans and spurred policymakers around the world to action.

It also troubled the supervisors for the largest public pension in the United States, setting off a debate last month about whether the funds they oversee might also be at risk — and what they should do about it.

With more than $600 billion in assets, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System had long invested heavily in Amazon, Facebook, Google, Nvidia and the vanguards of the dawning A.I. age. It was hardly alone in that embrace of Big Tech, and like many, its well-placed bets had yielded soaring returns benefiting its more than two million workers.

But the question of whether its investments had come at a cost seemed to weigh on the administrators of the California system, known as CalPERS, at a routine meeting in September. As they pored over the latest numbers, some on the board openly grappled with their responsibilities in a world in which A.I. could disrupt American life.

“The market is even more reliant now on tech than it has ever been. We have certainly prospered greatly over the last two decades from our investments there,” said Lisa Middleton, one of the board’s members. “That always raises the question: At what point do we need to start looking to what the downside could be?”

The moment in California underscored one of the great uncertainties in America’s grand economic transformation. For millions of workers, the fate of their hard-fought retirement savings may well hinge on the boom-or-bust potential of artificial intelligence.

At a time when technology giants dominate financial markets, the exuberance on Wall Street around A.I. has been to their benefit, sending stocks soaring and boosting retirement accounts accordingly. But that jubilation could just as easily turn to doubt, delivering a major blow to the money that many Americans rely on in older age.

The risks are evident in state and local retirement programs, which together serve more than 37 million people. In states like California, New York and Texas, the officials who oversee these funds have started to question their exposure to A.I. — and some have even turned away investments — out of fear that the sky-high financial returns may not last forever.

The work to protect retirees’ savings has not exactly been easy, given the financial needs of pension funds and the extent to which technology companies dominate financial markets. With the arrival of data centers, the ambitions of Silicon Valley have only expanded further into everything from energy to real estate — and, at times, Americans’ retirement savings have helped to supply the capital for these expensive endeavors.

With roughly $6 trillion in assets, the public pensions are “feeding the capacity of the A.I. companies to grow,” said Anthony Randazzo, the executive director of Equable Institute, a nonprofit that studies pensions. In an analysis of available data, his firm estimates that state and local retirement plans’ exposure to A.I.-related investments could be as high as $700 billion.

But, Mr. Randazzo said it raised many questions: “If there is a systematic reduction in the value of A.I. companies, how does that map onto all the rest of the assets of these plans? Does it take everything else down with it?”

For the moment, A.I. is powering Wall Street while setting the stage for highly anticipated public offerings from the likes of Anthropic, which unfurled details about its finances on Monday. The excitement has factored heavily into the thinking at the White House that it should refrain from issuing regulations that might slow down the industry.

“I will never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution,” President Trump said in late September.

Increasingly, though, there is worry that the excitement may not last. The concern stems from the otherworldly pace at which tech companies are constructing data centers and other related infrastructure, a set of investments that could reach $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032, according to a new paper from Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor and economist at Columbia University.

In one scenario, the A.I. investments could contribute heavily to the nation’s economic growth, making workers more productive. But there is also the possibility that sufficient demand — and revenue — do not materialize quickly enough to warrant all of the newly created computing resources, causing financial havoc.

The tension was top of mind when state and local retirement officials from around the country gathered in August for an annual industry forum, held in Chicago. Amid the sessions on pension finance and management, Paulo Carvão, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School, warned that A.I. was “entering the stress test period.”

In general, public pensions are funded through worker and employer contributions as well as investments. These retirement systems, on average, are able to fund about 86 percent of the benefits that they are obligated to pay, according to an October analysis from Equable, which described some funds’ finances as improving yet “fragile.”

After the conference, Mr. Carvão recalled that attendees had expressed a range of views about the promise and peril of A.I.: a skepticism about the technology, an eagerness to “increase my exposure” to its gains and even, at times, a concern about whether it was “morally acceptable” to support an industry that could displace the very workers whom pensions serve.

Nevertheless, Mr. Carvão said he emphasized there was a “lot of wealth created around” A.I., for now, but upheaval “could materially affect” pension finances.

Already, that concern about blowback has prompted some pension officials and the people they serve to question if they might be vulnerable to an A.I. bubble.

This June, for example, the retirement system for public workers in Los Angeles found that as much as 19 percent of its investment portfolio was directly implicated by artificial intelligence. Officials overseeing a retirement system for school employees in Ohio said in October that they were undertaking their own review.

One of the nation’s largest teachers unions wrote the Trump administration last month that it was “gravely concerned” for the pension savings of its nearly two million members, and it urged the federal government to rein in risky A.I. practices. And, in New York City, pension leaders grew troubled enough about A.I. concentration recently that they started looking differently at their own investments.

“You see a systemic level of risk that is making us wary,” said Mark Levine, who oversees the city’s pension systems as comptroller.

This year, New York City turned away a chance to invest about $250 million in a private equity fund involving small and medium-size A.I. companies. Mr. Levine declined to offer specifics, but said he passed on the pitch, which had good fundamentals, because he was “worried it was too concentrated in A.I.”

The cautiousness among some pension officials offers a stark contrast to the scramble by tech giants, chip makers and data center developers for the capital needed to build out artificial intelligence. To source that money, they have increasingly looked beyond their own balance sheets and adopted a series of novel, evolving and potentially risky A.I. financing tactics.

Much of that has involved debt, including bonds by cash-flush technology giants and other private debt deals that have supported a wide array of A.I., real estate and infrastructure projects. The many buyers include public pensions, which had been increasing their exposure to private capital and private equity even before the current boom.

“It’s a huge opportunity,” Christopher Sheldon, the co-head of credit and markets for KKR, an investment firm, said at a conference hosted by Barclays in September. Mr. Sheldon, whose firm is among the institutions raising capital for Nvidia and others, added that he expected “pension is going to follow” with interest.

The extent of the risk depends on the level and nature of the debt and other investments that pensions hold. Still, the trend has troubled watchdogs at the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform, two left-leaning advocacy groups.

In an October report, they warned that an A.I.-fueled downturn “would hit pension funds hard, particularly since A.I.-linked assets dominate stock and corporate bond markets as well.” Maya Jenkins, a senior policy analyst at Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund and one of the authors of the report, added that there was “an open question about who is going to absorb the losses should these large tech firms run into problems.”

For pension officials and the workers they serve, some of the anxiety stems from past crashes. That includes the global financial crisis, which delivered a major financial blow to public pensions, swelling the gap between their existing assets and future liabilities by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to David Draine, the principal officer with the state fiscal policy project at Pew Charitable Trusts.

It took states many years to recover, and some pensions in states like New Jersey and Illinois still suffer from severe shortfalls. Mr. Draine said another major economic calamity could force states to commit their own funds to plug any holes.

That painful history appeared to weigh on officials in Texas, who gathered in September to discuss the finances for a pension system that serves about two million local teachers.

Jase Auby, the program’s chief investment officer, began his presentation by highlighting the healthy growth of the system’s portfolio. But he eventually reached a slide comparing the A.I. boom with past periods of economic transformation, from electrification to the internet.

Some of those inflection points “ended in tears for the investment community,” acknowledged Mr. Auby, who described the current moment as a “cautionary tale” as tech giants pour huge sums into A.I.

His diagnosis: “So far, so good, actually.” But Mr. Auby added: “We’ll continue to monitor that and watch that, but history definitely is giving us some lessons here today.”

item.title: In the A.I. ‘Robogym,’ Machines Train to Be More Like Humans
item.description:
Neura Robotics is not a household name. It’s not even the most prominent business in Metzingen, a German town of 22,000 people that is also home to the fashion brand Hugo Boss.

But in just a few months, Neura’s founder, David Reger, has attracted investment from some of the world’s most powerful technology companies, including Nvidia and Amazon, and received invitations to meet the leaders of Europe’s three largest economies.

The company’s rise underscores the importance of artificial intelligence and robotics, technologies that could help Europe transform its ailing manufacturing sector and take on Chinese competition. Neura is among companies at the forefront of Europe’s efforts to seize the potential economic gains as A.I. makes the leap from the digital world to the physical.

“We are not efficient anymore,” said Mr. Reger, who raised as much as $1.4 billion in June. “But I do believe that this can be solved.”

Whether A.I.-powered robots can live up to their promise remains unclear. Companies need to teach them to perform complex tasks, a challenge that requires the collection of vast amounts of data.

European robots are also far outnumbered.

After rolling out 2.3 million industrial robots, almost half the global fleet, China is moving into the next frontier. Unlike the mostly one-armed machines that have been used for decades to perform repetitive tasks, the next generation of robots is expected to see, hear, feel and — most important — learn.

One of the keys to Europe’s strategy is a tech hub on the edge of Munich Airport. Inside the facility, as many as 100 humanoids and other robots have embarked on a 24-7 training mission. On a recent morning, a day after joining business leaders in Berlin for a discussion with Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany and Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain, Mr. Reger opened the “robogym” to a journalist for the first time. He declined to provide details of the meetings with the government leaders.

Wearing a black blazer, a black shirt and black pants, Mr. Reger, 38, introduced the team. The robots picked up car parts and placed them into containers, stacked boxes and carried out other tasks, mimicking the movements of human trainers who guided them remotely. One robot practiced tightening its grip on a glass, learning how to respond when water is added.

When one robot learns a new skill, they all get smarter as the data is fed into a cloud-based platform, or a shared brain. Neura has signed up dozens of automotive, logistics, pharmaceutical and other companies to carry out their own training in the gym, declining to identify them. More than 2,600 have applied for space in one of the sites, Neura’s chief said.

The training center, developed with the Technical University of Munich, is part of a wider plan. By the end of the year, Neura aims to have five gyms operating globally, including one already opened in Hangzhou, China. Ten more are expected to follow.

Unlike generative A.I. models trained on enormous amounts of internet data, physical A.I. depends on the costly collection of real-world data. Mr. Reger likened it to learning how to swim. You can’t simply watch videos; you have to get in the water.

China, however, is building most of the pools.

More than 90 humanoid data collection centers are running across China, according to Interact Analysis, a consulting firm. And the campaign, fueled by state support and a need to replace retiring workers, shows no signs of slowing down. At least 50 more sites are under development. Europe has fewer than 10 facilities.

It’s not just the scale of China’s operation that is making headlines. A Chinese humanoid in August broke Usain Bolt’s record in a 100-meter sprint, while dozens of others ran a half-marathon in Beijing. At the Paris Motor Show, robots developed by China’s Agibot danced to the Dua Lipa song “Levitating.”

“The skill is undeniable, but a lot of it, especially in the humanoid sector, is around what we’d call entertainment robots versus industrial robots,” said Arnaud Robert, the president of Hexagon Robotics, a Swiss company that is working on a pilot with BMW at one of the German automaker’s plants in Leipzig.

That leaves an opening for European companies, he said.

A.I. robots are hitting the factory floor in Europe for the first time, with Germany emerging as the main training ground. Robots are expected to move into production at the BMW site by the first quarter of next year. Agile Robots, in Munich, is working with partners including Google DeepMind. Another company, Humanoid, aims to integrate robots into the operations of Schaeffler, a German auto supplier, by the end of 2026.

While Neura advances with the gyms, it is teaming up with another supplier, Bosch, and other companies, equipping more than 1,000 workers with sensor suits to record their movements and capture other data during their regular shifts.

European companies want to be judged on their ability to develop technology that translates into tangible results. But they will need to prove that their robots can operate safely and efficiently — and at a low enough cost to make them economically viable.

Smart robots in factories, warehouses, hospitals and hotels are forecast to play a critical role as countries cope with aging populations and shrinking work forces. The number of humanoids deployed worldwide could rise to one million in 2030 from 15,000 last year, if costs fall and the technology does not encounter regulatory headwinds, said Zornitsa Todorova, a researcher at Barclays.

“The next 10 years will be the decade of the robot — and at the moment, it looks like that decade might belong to China,” Ms. Todorova said. Still, Europe’s focus on safety and expertise in hardware, such as actuators that enable robots to move, provide an edge, she said.

Neura raised funds this year from several prominent companies, including existing partners Nvidia and Amazon. Leading the investment was Tether, the cryptocurrency company, which is valued at more than $180 billion and has faced scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators. Neura said part of the $1.4 billion was tied to milestones that it was on track to achieve.

Growing up as the eldest of 11 siblings in Rottweil, 50 miles from Metzingen, Mr. Reger dreamed of living overseas, eventually heading to California. Instead of finding a tech job in Silicon Valley, however, he got his start working with a Christian organization to help homeless people in San Francisco.

After returning home, he developed a deeper appreciation for Europe and its health and social systems. Rather than attending a university, he taught himself engineering and got a job in Switzerland, where he built his first robots.

Mr. Reger, who also met with France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, in September, said he aimed to become “Europe’s largest taxpayer,” combining A.I. and robotics to help create an economic engine for Europe that is even bigger than the car industry. Failing to reap the gains, he said, would be costly.

“This is a competition,” Mr. Reger said. “If you see other countries get more efficient through robotics and we don’t, it’s going to be very difficult to come out of this situation.”

item.title: Holiday Travel Costs Are Soaring. 5 Ways to Save.
item.description:
Last summer, when Melissa Cuomo and her family began looking at round-trip flights from New York to Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic for a holiday getaway, they assumed the $2,000-a-ticket price in the main cabin would come down. It never did.

A few months later, when the flights rose to $3,000 each, Ms. Cuomo, a teacher who lives in Roslyn Harbor, N.Y., was scouring the internet for alternatives when she spotted a number to call for group rates on JetBlue when traveling with 10 or more people. For their family of 15, she secured rates of just over $1,000 a ticket, saving approximately $30,000.

“Maybe we should have been doing this all along, but it was never necessary before,” Ms. Cuomo said.

The family’s challenge illustrates the state of travel over the 2026 holidays: Prices are up, but the determined are finding creative ways to go, whether at Thanksgiving, Christmas or during the week leading up to New Year’s Day.

Four in 10 consumers planned to travel this season, according to a holiday outlook report from the consulting firm PwC, down slightly from last year. Among those with travel plans, 38 percent said they planned to economize by staying in budget or midrange hotels.

“The desire hasn’t gone away,” said Jonathan Kletzel, the U.S. travel, transportation and logistics sector leader at PwC. Instead, he noted planning patterns such as: early booking, flexible reservations, and rebooking without penalty when travelers found a better post-purchase price.

All signs point to more expensive holiday travel, but with persistence, flexibility and creativity, there are ways to save.

On average, airfares are up more than 22 percent in September compared with a year ago, according to the most recent Consumer Price Index.

While the increase is largely attributed to fuel costs that have spiked since the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran that began in February, travelers shopping for Thanksgiving flights have seen some prices double, compounded by demand.

Data from the flight search engine Kayak showed that domestic airfares were up an average of about $100 from 2025 rates five weeks before Thanksgiving. The travel booking app Hopper put the average domestic round-trip at $389 a ticket, 39 percent more than last year.

Remaining flexible on the dates you fly can pay dividends. Kayak recommended flying on Thanksgiving Day itself to save up to 19 percent over peak fares.

Flexibility also applies to where you fly. Katy Nastro, the aviation and travel correspondent for Flighty, a flight-tracking app, noted that airlines this holiday season have increased flights from hub to hub, favoring routes between major cities at the expense of smaller cities, where service may be curtailed.

She suggested considering flights between major airports and filling in the gaps with buses, trains or rental cars. Bargain shoppers should also price one-way flights on other carriers, and use miles to pay for the flight.

“If you’re looking for affordability this late in the game, you might need to make concessions,” Ms. Nastro said. One concession might be a connecting flight. According to Points Path, a website that evaluates flight prices in points and miles, nonstop flights cost about 20 percent more on average than connecting itineraries.

Getting creative may involve forms of transportation other than flying. In PwC’s holiday report, a third of holiday travelers planned to skip flying.

The cost of driving has surged, too. The average price of gas is $4.29 a gallon nationally according to AAA, compared with $3.19 last Thanksgiving. Financially, the appeal of driving grows with the number of travelers in one vehicle.

Using the average car, which gets 25.6 miles per gallon, according to the U.S. Department of Energy, gas for a 400-mile trip between New York and Pittsburgh would cost about $134 round trip. Google Maps puts the drive at about six and a half hours, excluding rest stops. By comparison, a nonstop flight between the two cities over the long Thanksgiving weekend, which takes about an hour and 40 minutes, excluding airport time, recently started at around $450 round trip, according to Google Flights.

The bus company FlixBus takes roughly nine hours to drive between New York and Pittsburgh. A recent round-trip ticket on the route started around $100.

Traveling the route by Amtrak train takes approximately nine and a half hours and was recently priced around $225 round trip.

Even the cheaper ground options are up from a year ago. Omio, a multimodal booking service that searches air as well as train and bus schedules, found that rates booked Thanksgiving through Christmas so far this year were up 29 percent for flights, 22 percent for trains and 15 percent for buses.

Since air and ground options involve a trade-off between time and money, consider pricing one-way travel on each and combining transportation methods.

“Usually when it comes to convenience versus price, convenience will be the loser,” Ms. Nastro said.

If you intend to travel over Christmas, book quickly. Points Path found that the best time to book a Christmas trip was about 56 days before departure, with a low-price window running 33 to 67 days out, or right now.

“Oftentimes, people will book Thanksgiving before Halloween, and wait to book their Christmas trip until the week of Thanksgiving or the week after,” said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper. “You don’t want to do that this year. There will be very expensive fares if you wait too long.”

Hopper said the current domestic round-trip at Christmas averaged $452, up 22 percent over last year.

For a few weeks post-Thanksgiving, there’s generally a lull in travel until Christmas week. If you can move your trip to mid-December, you’ll save.

This year, the ski industry is contending with a “snow hangover” generated by last year’s dry conditions in the West, depressing early season bookings amid the uncertainty of this year’s El Nino weather pattern.

“It seems people are hedging their snow bets to give it a bit of time to fill in,” said Cat Iwanchuk, the vice president of business development at Ski.com, a mountain travel agency.

She identified Canadian resorts like Banff and Lake Louise as popular for greater “snow security” and a good exchange rate (the U.S. dollar is worth 1.40 Canadian dollars).

Prices for Caribbean cruises in December are down 8 percent year over year, according to Cruise Critic, a review and booking site, which it attributes to the growth in capacity in the region. The site recently published a seven-night Holland America cruise deal from Fort Lauderdale leaving Dec. 19 starting at $699 a person.

Timeshare companies note that travelers can save by preparing meals in their rentals. GoTimesharing is offering 20 percent off rentals in resorts from Vermont to Hawaii on bookings made until Dec. 15 (use the promo code HomeAwayFromHome).

Many travelers book extended vacations between Christmas and New Year’s Day — the period that the industry calls “festive season,” when demand and rates spike.

“At top ski and beach properties, availability is already tight,” said Lucie Kittel, the founder of Domino Travel, based in Samford, Conn.

Contributing to higher costs, many resorts impose minimum stays of five or more nights during the holidays. Ms. Kittel recommends destinations in Asia for value.

“Bangkok, for example, can be surprisingly reasonable over Christmas, while places like Zermatt and Courchevel command a significant premium that week,” she said, naming popular European ski resorts.

In the third quarter, searches for North American travel over Christmas on Expedia were up 5 percent, with the largest gains among less-obvious destinations such as Quebec City and San Pedro Sula in Honduras.

“Demand is not disappearing; it is redistributing,” Melanie Fish, the vice president of global public relations at Expedia Group Brands, wrote in an email.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: The Scariest Part of Halloween This Year? The Candy Prices.
item.description:
The economy has come for Tami Adolphson’s Halloween candy bowl.

Prices are so high this year that she considered turning off the porch light at her home near Salt Lake City and ignoring the doorbell. Ms. Adolphson, 63, and her husband, Lee, 68, closed down their trucking company and retired last year. The household budget is tight.

“We’re finding it harder to justify big prices even for the extremely satisfying ritual of handing out candy to kids,” she said. “We are not going to dip into savings for Halloween candy.”

But she couldn’t stand missing out. “I just can’t turn off the lights on these children, she said. So last week she went to Costco and spent $21.39 on a bag of 90 mixed chocolate bars.

“We just won’t eat out one time this month,” she said. “It’s worth it to keep the tradition.”

Anyone who has been to the grocery store recently has noticed higher prices. The cost of vegetables has jumped by 6 percent since last year. Beef is up by about 9 percent. But the price of Halloween candy — particularly chocolate — is even scarier.

One recent analysis of the prices on 17 popular Halloween candy varieties showed a 15 percent jump from last year. The average price of a 100-piece bag is $16.96, up a staggering 71 percent since 2021, according to FinanceBuzz, a digital media company. Google searches for “cheap Halloween candy bulk” and “where to buy cheap Halloween candy” are up more than 5,000 percent year-over-year, said Megan Stoner, a spokeswoman for the company.

“The prices have gotten completely out of hand,” said Renni Turpin, 30. This is her first Halloween in a new neighborhood in Charlotte, N.C., and she wants to make a good impression. “No one wants to be the ‘raisin house,’” she said.

She would like to be the king-size candy bar house, but she works at a school and recently purchased her home. Even buying slightly less expensive candy, she figures she’ll spend about $100, or what she might spend on a week’s worth of groceries.

“It means that the Halloween tradition is now a financial burden,” she said. We asked New York Times readers if the price of candy was changing how they would approach trick-or-treating this year. More than 200 people responded, and almost 90 percent of them said they were adjusting their approach because the price of candy was so high. They are buying less, shopping sales and heading to bargain grocery outlets. Candy bowls are being cut with small bags of salty snacks, temporary tattoos, Play-Doh and low-cost trinkets they can buy in bulk.

And then there is the classic method for stretching a small candy budget: Limit how many pieces a child (or rowdy teenager) can take.

Already, Halloween candy sales for the month ending Oct. 17 are down 6 percent compared with the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm.

Some people are abandoning the classic chocolate offerings. A climate-driven global cacao supply crisis sent prices to record highs in 2025, and companies began formulating their chocolate with less expensive ingredients and selling smaller packages of candy for more money. A bag of Reese’s miniatures that weighed 17.6 ounces last year weighs 15.8 ounces now and costs $1.50 more, according to analysts at the web research company Apify.

Luckily, Sour Patch Kids, Skittles and Nerd Gummy Clusters are less expensive and climbing in popularity among younger generations, who are turning away from chocolate in favor of candies with texture and sour or tangy flavors, said Sally Lyon Wyatt, an executive vice president for consumer goods and food service insights at Mintel, the market research firm.

“People will celebrate Halloween, but they’re going to use different tactics to do it,” she said. “Candy might be part of it, but maybe not as much as it had been in the past. There’s just going to be a bit more creativity.”

Cynthia Thomasset, who lives in Shillington, Pa., will likely supplement her candy stash with school supplies and stickers. She plans to have plenty on hand because her suburban neighborhood draws children from a nearby area that is one of the poorest in Pennsylvania.

But there will be no leftovers. “Usually I panic and go buy more right before,” she said, “but this year I am going to give out what I have and that’s it.”

Some households are getting even more creative. “I’ve switched to passing out ramen,” said Angie Vasey, a teacher who lives in Round Lake, Ill. The packets of instant soup were on sale this year for 10 cents apiece.

Magen Pillar, a communications director for United Way, is buying a $25 bag of candy and supplementing the holiday by building a bonfire and handing out bowls of her husband, Matt’s, homemade beef and bean chili from the driveway of their home in Columbus, Ind. It’s an inexpensive way to build a little neighborhood esprit de corps.

“It is hard to believe that a pot of chili is cheaper than a bag of candy,” she said.

Traditionalists remain, including those dedicated to making Halloween as special as they can with the ultimate prize: full-size candy bars.

Mitch Collins, 71, bought a mix of 270 Snickers, KitKats and other chocolate and packages of Skittles and Starbursts to hand out in his neighborhood in Oakdale, Calif.

“As a child, one time I received a full-size bar on Halloween,” he said. “I remember it to this day and want to share that joy with the kids that come to our home.”

He shelled out $269 at Costco.

“Yeah, it costs a lot,” he said, “but their joy is worth it.”
